source.title: Shaping capabilities with token-level data filtering

record.tranche_reason: Measures held-out text loss across compute scales, using compute-to-loss curves as in scaling-law studies, but in the new setting of pretraining data filtering.
record.gate_note: The study reports cross-entropy compute-to-loss curves and loss-matched compute slowdowns. Its medical benchmark results are not additional scaling-law rows: the multiple-choice and free-response evaluations are reported for 1.8B models, not as scaling sweeps. The classifier F1 results are also outside the claim.
record.test_reason: The study trains compute-optimal series from 61M to 1.8B parameters (about 1e18–1e20 FLOPs) and plots held-out cross-entropy against compute. It calls the baseline and filtered curves compute-to-loss power laws and reports that removing a domain from pretraining data lowers the exponent on that domain. This is a new setting (pretraining data filtering) with results on the power-law form (V1) and on its data dependence (V7). The headline 7000× slowdown measures the study's own intervention, not the scaling law.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that token filtering Pareto-dominates document filtering and gets more effective with pretraining compute (7000× slowdown at 1.8B). It is robust to adversarial finetuning, does not harm alignment, and works with imperfect labels. They note filtered models 'scale worse' on the forget domain (lower exponent), warn that scaling could turn U-shaped at larger scale, and call for testing beyond 7B.
record.recipe_differences: Measures held-out cross-entropy versus compute, but focuses on the effects of filtering medical content rather than estimating general-purpose scaling laws; uses loss-matched compute slowdown and filtered-data comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: Filtering method changes the forget-domain scaling exponent and loss-matched slowdown; filtering effectiveness depends on label error and on when filtering begins.

fits_no_version.finding: Filtering effectiveness, measured as loss-matched compute slowdown, grows with scale: 7000× for token removal and about 30× for document filtering at 1.8B. It is about an order of magnitude weaker when filtering is delayed by 40% of training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relative scaling laws: the effective-compute penalty of removing a domain from pretraining grows with compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Compute slowdown falls off as a power law in simulated classifier label error rate, saturating at high error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-filtering effectiveness scales as a power law in label noise.

record.problems: The scaling-law evidence is limited to compute-to-loss sweeps in the paper’s medical capability-shaping setup, over the reported compute range. Several plotted loss values are not stated numerically, and the largest-model slowdown is estimated by interpolation of the baseline log-log compute-to-loss plot.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 16 plots loss curves for medical, biology, and non-medical text across all filtering series; only the medical-domain curves were retained as rows because the text specifically describes the forget-domain exponent change. Other separate per-size plot points and the Figure 12 noise-level series were not extracted as individual rows; the latter is summarized by the stated trend in r8.

untested.parts: Scaling in parameters or tokens separately with the others not limiting; more than about two orders of magnitude; any fitted exponent values.
Extrapolation from small fits to much larger runs is not tested.
The study assumes Hoffmann compute-optimal allocation (it trains 'compute-optimal Transformers') but does not test it.
Width-to-depth ratio is held fixed at 64; shape is not varied.
No other modalities. Adversarial-finetuning tokens versus scale concern robustness, not a fine-tuning loss scaling law.
Multiple-choice and free-response evaluations are at 1.8B only; no downstream scale sweep.
Parameter counting, schedule and fitting method are not tested; only data composition (domain filtering) is varied.

missing.what: Retain-domain (biology, non-medical) compute-to-loss curves for the baseline and filtered series. These bear on V1 (baseline power law on other held-out domains) and on V7 (whether retain exponents change). Declared in rows_left_out but needed for cross-study comparison.
Aggressive-filtering and classifier-quality sweeps (Figures 13, 27, 28) showing the scaling trend shifts with the fraction of tokens filtered and with classifier quality.

record.verdict_notes: Scaling-law evidence is incidental to a capability-shaping paper. The baseline curve is interpolated piecewise in log-log space rather than fitted, and no exponents or fit quality are reported. V1 support is therefore weak and figure-based over about two orders of magnitude. Compute-optimal (Chinchilla) allocation is assumed, not tested.

versions.untested_parts: Tests compute-to-loss behavior on medical, biology, and non-medical text in filtered and unfiltered pretraining. Does not separately test loss scaling with parameter count or training tokens while holding other factors fixed.
Does not test whether fits on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
Does not compare loss-minimising parameter/token allocations at fixed compute.
Does not vary depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
Does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling laws.
Does not report downstream task performance as a scale sweep or relate downstream performance to pretraining loss across scales.

Tests sensitivity to filtering conditions, label noise, and when filtering begins. Does not test parameter-counting choices, alternative curve-fitting methods, or disagreement between published scaling-law fits.

rows.subject: unfiltered model series
rows.measure: Held-out text cross-entropy loss versus pretraining compute.
rows.note: The paper plots the unfiltered compute-to-loss curve and uses it to estimate loss-matched compute; point values are not given in text.
rows.check: Figure-only, but §B.1 states the baseline follows a compute-to-loss power law (Lb ∝ Cb^-α). The paper only linearly interpolates the log-log plot; no fitted exponent is reported. The range is about two orders of magnitude, so 'observed' rests on the authors' description.

rows.subject: token loss masking model series
rows.operation_detail: Compute-to-loss sweep with loss masking on forget-domain tokens.
rows.measure: Held-out text cross-entropy loss versus pretraining compute.
rows.baseline: unfiltered model series; exact values not stated
rows.note: The authors state that filtered series have a lower-magnitude compute-to-loss exponent on the forget domain than the baseline.
rows.check: Measures loss on a domain masked from training, not held-out pretraining-distribution loss, so it bears on V7 (data dependence of the exponent), not V1. The exponent change is stated qualitatively only; figure-only.

rows.subject: token removal model series
rows.operation_detail: Compute-to-loss sweep after replacing forget tokens with a hidden token and masking their loss.
rows.measure: Held-out text cross-entropy loss versus pretraining compute.
rows.baseline: unfiltered model series; exact values not stated
rows.note: The authors state that filtered series have a lower-magnitude compute-to-loss exponent on the forget domain than the baseline.
rows.check: Same as r2: forget-domain loss under token removal; the lower exponent is stated in §B.1 and the Figure 16 caption, with no numbers. Not a V1 row.

rows.subject: document filtering model series
rows.operation_detail: Compute-to-loss sweep after filtering medical documents.
rows.measure: Held-out text cross-entropy loss versus pretraining compute.
rows.baseline: unfiltered model series; exact values not stated
rows.note: The authors state that filtered series have a lower-magnitude compute-to-loss exponent on the forget domain than the baseline.
rows.check: Same as r2, for document filtering. Not a V1 row.

rows.subject: token removal model series
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute required by an unfiltered run to match filtered-model loss.
rows.measure: Loss-matched compute slowdown relative to unfiltered training.
rows.value: 7000× compute slowdown for the largest models
rows.note: The paper reports that filtering becomes more effective with scale and gives the 7000× figure for the largest models.
rows.check: Loss-matched compute slowdown (7000×) measures the study's own intervention, derived by interpolating the baseline curve. It is not a measurement of loss scaling itself.

rows.subject: document filtering model series
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute required by an unfiltered run to match filtered-model loss.
rows.measure: Loss-matched compute slowdown relative to unfiltered training.
rows.value: around 30× compute slowdown for the largest models
rows.note: The authors report that document filtering also becomes more effective with scale, but less so than token removal.
rows.check: Same as r5: a filtering-effectiveness metric (about 30× for document filtering), not a scaling-law result.

rows.subject: token loss masking model series
rows.operation_detail: Varied the point during training when loss masking began.
rows.measure: Effectiveness of filtering relative to an unfiltered baseline.
rows.value: delaying filtering by 40% makes it around an order of magnitude less effective
rows.note: The onset of filtering changes the effectiveness of the scaling result.
rows.check: Filter onset versus filtering effectiveness is about the intervention's training dynamics. It does not bear on fitting choices or on the form of the loss scaling law.

rows.subject: token loss masking model series
rows.operation_detail: Artificially flipped classifier labels at varying rates, then measured compute slowdown.
rows.measure: Compute slowdown as a function of label error rate.
rows.value: Power-law scaling in compute slowdown; small increases in error substantially reduce filtering in the low-error regime, with saturation at high error
rows.note: This reports sensitivity of the filtering scaling relationship to noisy labels.
rows.check: Power-law relation between classifier error rate and compute slowdown. This is not loss versus parameters, data or compute, and it is sensitivity of the intervention, not of scaling-law fits.

relationships.condition: Unfiltered compute-optimal GPT-2-style models, 61M–1.8B, about 1e18–1e20 FLOPs, held-out PubMed/bioRxiv/arXiv text
relationships.reason: r1: the authors describe the baseline compute-to-loss curve as a power law and use it for interpolation. The evidence is figure-only, with no fit statistics, over roughly two orders of magnitude.
relationships.display_finding: The baseline compute-to-loss curve is described as a power law and used for interpolation across roughly two orders of magnitude.
